title: Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell, Feminist Physician
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell, the first licensed woman physician in America. They cover her Quaker upbringing in England and her father Samuel Blackwell's sugar business and death in Cincinnati; her decision to become a doctor after a dying friend said a woman doctor might have helped her; her years teaching in the South; her admission to Geneva Medical College in 1847 as a supposed prank and her graduation first in class; her work in Paris and London, including the loss of sight in one eye and her friendship with Florence Nightingale; her hygiene and prevention advocacy; founding the New York Infirmary for Women and Children with sister Emily Blackwell and a women's medical college; co-founding the London School of Medicine for Women; her views on women's morality and abortion; and her later illness and death in 1910. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from Isaac, a seventh grader in Seattle during quarantine, and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Blackwell
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show's intro and introduce Elizabeth Blackwell as America's first woman physician, noting her Quaker family and her pioneering path.

segments.title: Blackwell family, Quaker background and father's sugar business
segments.summary: Blackwell is born near Bristol, England, the third of nine children to Quaker parents Samuel and Hannah Blackwell. Samuel, a sugar refiner, hires tutors to teach daughters like sons and avoids physical punishment. After his refinery fails, the family moves to New York, then Cincinnati, where Samuel dies of fever in 1838, leaving them poor.

segments.title: Decision to become a doctor
segments.summary: Blackwell resolves to be self-sufficient and never marry. She decides to become a doctor after a dying friend says a woman doctor might have treated her better, despite her own aversion to anatomy.

segments.title: Teaching in the South and rejection from medical schools
segments.summary: Blackwell teaches in Kentucky, then in North and South Carolina, saving money for medical school and teaching Sunday school to enslaved children. She is rejected by many medical schools and is mentored informally by Southern physicians.

segments.title: Admission to Geneva Medical College
segments.summary: After applying to many schools, Blackwell is accepted to Geneva Medical College in 1847 at age 26. Classmates reportedly voted, believing it was a prank, and the Boston Medical Journal covered her arrival.

segments.title: Medical school experience and graduation
segments.summary: Blackwell faces hostility and gradually earns respect from professors and classmates. She graduates first in her class, and the dean reportedly bows to her at the diploma ceremony.

segments.title: Paris, London, hygiene advocacy and loss of eye
segments.summary: Blackwell practices in Paris and London, where she is steered toward midwifery and promotes handwashing and prevention, which is dismissed under miasma theory. She loses sight in her left eye from purulent ophthalmia after treating an infected infant. In London she befriends Florence Nightingale.

segments.title: New York Infirmary and women's medical education
segments.summary: Back in New York, Blackwell is denied a dispensary post and opens her own clinic. With sister Emily and Marie Zakrzewska she founds the New York Infirmary for Women and Children, which adds a medical college in 1868, with Emily handling surgery.
topics: New York Infirmary for Women and Children

segments.title: Feminism, Victorian morality and later career in England
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Blackwell's Victorian-style feminism and moral views, including opposition to abortion. Blackwell moves to London, co-founds the London School of Medicine for Women with Sophia Jex Blake and Elizabeth Garrett Anderson, and becomes the first woman on the English medical register. She later stops practicing due to gallstones and dies in 1910 after a 1907 fall.
topics: London School of Medicine for Women

segments.title: Listener mail from Isaac
segments.summary: Isaac, a seventh grader in Seattle in quarantine, writes in to say the show helps him through the coronavirus stay-at-home period. The hosts chat about video games, including Red Dead Redemption, and sign off with mail instructions.
